title: Design a data structure that accepts a continuous stream of numbers and can return the median of all numbers seen so far at any time. Insertion and median-query should both be efficient. Explain the two-heap technique.
shortTitle: Find the Median of a Number Stream (Two Heaps)

s1_definition.profdef: Find the Median of a Number Stream is the canonical Two Heaps problem. We keep a max-heap holding the smaller half of the numbers and a min-heap holding the larger half, balanced so their sizes differ by at most one. The median is then either the top of the larger heap, or the average of the two tops when the counts are equal. Each insertion costs logarithmic time for the heap operations, and a median query costs constant time by peeking at the heap tops.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, transaction amounts arrive all day, and the risk team wants the running median amount at any moment to spot drift. We split the amounts into two buckets: a low bucket that always holds the smaller half with its largest value on top, and a high bucket that holds the larger half with its smallest value on top. The middle of all amounts sits right at the boundary between the two buckets, so we read it off the tops instantly.
s1_definition.oneliner: Smaller half in a max-heap, larger half in a min-heap, keep them balanced, and the median lives at the boundary.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Find the Median of a Number Stream is the canonical Two Heaps problem. We keep a max-heap holding the smaller half of the numbers and a min-heap holding the larger half, balanced so their sizes differ by at most one. The median is then either the top of the larger heap, or the average of the two tops when the counts are equal. Each insertion costs logarithmic time for the heap operations, and a median query costs constant time by peeking at the heap tops.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, transaction amounts arrive all day, and the risk team wants the running median amount at any moment to spot drift. We split the amounts into two buckets: a low bucket that always holds the smaller half with its largest value on top, and a high bucket that holds the larger half with its smallest value on top. The middle of all amounts sits right at the boundary between the two buckets, so we read it off the tops instantly.

**One line to remember:** Smaller half in a max-heap, larger half in a min-heap, keep them balanced, and the median lives at the boundary.

sections.s2_technical:
On each insertion we first decide which heap the number belongs in. A common rule is: if the max-heap (smaller half) is empty or the number is at most its top, push to the max-heap, otherwise push to the min-heap. For example, `if (maxHeap.isEmpty() || num <= maxHeap.peek()) maxHeap.offer(num); else minHeap.offer(num);`.

Then we rebalance so the heaps never differ by more than one element. If the max-heap has grown two larger than the min-heap, we move its top over, and vice versa. For example, `if (maxHeap.size() > minHeap.size() + 1) minHeap.offer(maxHeap.poll());`. This keeps the boundary exactly in the middle.

To read the median, if the heaps are equal in size the median is the average of the two tops, otherwise it is the top of the larger heap. A senior-level nuance in a banking context is that amounts are `BigDecimal`, so the max-heap uses `Comparator.reverseOrder()` and the average is computed with `BigDecimal` division at a controlled scale and rounding mode, never floating-point. Another nuance is that this streaming structure is far better than re-sorting on every query, which would be O(n log n) per query.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India processes a continuous stream of transaction amounts, and the risk team must see the running median amount at any instant to detect when typical transaction sizes drift. Sorting all amounts on every query would be far too slow for a live stream. This is exactly how the Two Heaps median structure works: it keeps the stream split so the median is always at the boundary.

Problem 2 — The stream never stops, so the structure must absorb each new amount cheaply and answer the median instantly. This is why insertion is a logarithmic heap operation and the query is a constant-time peek, rather than a full re-sort.

The code defines a `RunningMedian` class holding a max-heap and a min-heap of `BigDecimal`. It exposes `addAmount(BigDecimal)` and `median()`. A `Demo` feeds a stream of amounts for the National Bank of India and logs the running median after each insertion.

sections.s5_journey:
Input stream: 500, 1500, 1000, 3000, 250.

Step 1: Add 500. Max-heap empty, so 500 goes to the max-heap. Sizes 1 and 0, odd, median is the max-heap top, 500.

Step 2: Add 1500. 1500 is greater than the top 500, so it goes to the min-heap. Sizes 1 and 1, even, median is the average of 500 and 1500, which is 750.00.

Step 3: Add 1000. 1000 is greater than 500, so it goes to the min-heap, making min-heap {1000, 1500}. Now min-heap is larger by one, so move its top 1000 back to the max-heap. Max-heap {500, 1000}, min-heap {1500}. Odd, median is the max-heap top, 1000.

Step 4: Add 3000. Greater than 1000, goes to the min-heap {1500, 3000}. Sizes 2 and 2, even, median is the average of tops 1000 and 1500, which is 1250.00.

Step 5: Add 250. At most 1000, goes to the max-heap {500, 1000, 250}. Max-heap now larger by two, move its top 1000 to the min-heap. Max-heap {500, 250}, min-heap {1000, 1500, 3000}. Odd, median is the min-heap... no: min-heap is larger so we already rebalanced to keep max-heap holding the extra only when it is bigger; here min-heap size 3 exceeds max-heap size 2, so move min-heap top 1000 to max-heap, making max-heap {500, 250, 1000} and min-heap {1500, 3000}. Median is max-heap top, 1000.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Find the Median of a Number Stream is the textbook Two Heaps problem. I keep a max-heap that holds the smaller half of all numbers and a min-heap that holds the larger half, and I keep their sizes within one of each other. The median then lives exactly at the boundary: when the counts are equal it is the average of the two heap tops, and when they differ it is the top of the larger heap. Each insertion is a logarithmic heap operation and each median query is a constant-time peek, which is vastly better than re-sorting the whole stream on every query.

The mechanics I describe are: on insertion I place the number in the correct heap based on the current max-heap top, then I rebalance by moving a top element across if one heap grew two larger than the other. In a banking context I stress that amounts are BigDecimal, so the max-heap uses a reverse-order comparator and the even-count median is computed with BigDecimal division at a fixed scale and rounding mode, never floating-point, because money must stay exact.

At the National Bank of India I used this to maintain the running median transaction amount over a live stream, so the risk team could watch for drift in typical transaction sizes in real time. I absorbed each amount with a logarithmic insertion and answered the median instantly from the heap tops, keeping the heaps balanced so the boundary stayed in the middle. Explaining the balance invariant and the money-safe averaging is what shows an interviewer that I can turn the Two Heaps idea into a correct streaming structure for real financial data.
